<!-- slide 66 -->
# Showing Distributions {.divider}

[Boxplots, violins & ridgelines · Day 01]{.eyebrow}


<!-- slide 67 -->
## When & Why a Boxplot {.smaller}

[Distributions · when to use]{.eyebrow}

### A boxplot summarises spread, pick the chart that fits your question

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Use a boxplot to compare the **distribution** of a continuous value across a few
groups — its centre, spread, and outliers — without plotting every point.

**Spread is not precision.** SD describes how the data scatter around the mean;
SE describes how precise your estimate of the mean is. A boxplot answers the
first question; error bars on a mean answer the second.

```python
r = np.random.default_rng(1)
groups = ["WT", "Mut A", "Mut B"]
data = [r.normal(50, 6, 70),                # WT
        r.normal(62, 10, 70),               # Mut A — bigger spread
        r.normal(58, 4, 70)]                # Mut B — tighter
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 5
r = np.random.default_rng(1)
groups = ["WT", "Mut A", "Mut B"]
data = [r.normal(50, 6, 70), r.normal(62, 10, 70), r.normal(58, 4, 70)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5))
bp = ax.boxplot(data, widths=0.55, patch_artist=True, labels=groups)
for p in bp["boxes"]: p.set_facecolor(ECON["hongkong"][3]); p.set_edgecolor(GREEN)
for m in bp["medians"]: m.set_color(INK); m.set_linewidth(2)
for w in bp["whiskers"] + bp["caps"]: w.set_color(GREEN)
for fl in bp["fliers"]: fl.set(marker="o", markerfacecolor=CREAM, markeredgecolor=RED, markersize=5)
ax.set_ylabel("Expression (TPM)")
ax.set_title("DISTRIBUTION ACROSS THREE GENOTYPES", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=INK, pad=10)
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
SD vs SE: spread of the **data** vs precision of the **estimate**. Same numbers,
different question, different chart. *(Wilke 2019, Ch. 9)*
:::

## Building a Boxplot · Step 2: the raw points {.smaller}

### Look at the data first, with a little horizontal jitter

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Plot every observation, jittering x-position so points don't stack on one line.
This shows the sample size and shape that a summary will later hide.

```python {code-line-numbers="2-7"}

    ax.scatter(x, d,
               color=GREEN, s=18,
               alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none")
```

### Hide duplicate outliers, title the finding

:::: {.columns}

The points already show every value, so turn off the default flier markers.

<!-- slide 73 -->
## When & Why a Violin {.smaller}

[Distributions · when to use]{.eyebrow}

### Reach for a violin when the shape matters, not just the summary

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
A boxplot hides shape — two very different distributions can share the same
five-number summary. A violin draws a **mirrored density**, so a second hump or
a long skew is visible at a glance.

Use it when the distribution might be **bimodal** or strongly skewed. Use a
plain boxplot when a clean five-number summary is all you need.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 5
r = np.random.default_rng(3)
bimodal = np.concatenate([r.normal(45, 5, 45), r.normal(62, 5, 35)])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5))
vp = ax.violinplot([bimodal], positions=[1], widths=0.7, showextrema=False)
for b in vp["bodies"]:
    b.set_facecolor(ECON["hongkong"][3]); b.set_edgecolor(GREEN); b.set_alpha(0.85)
bx = ax.boxplot([bimodal], positions=[1], widths=0.12, patch_artist=True, showfliers=False)
for p in bx["boxes"]: p.set_facecolor(INK)
for m in bx["medians"]: m.set_color(CREAM)
ax.set_xticks([1]); ax.set_xticklabels(["one sample"]); ax.set_ylabel("Expression (TPM)")
ax.set_title("THE BOX MISSES THE TWO PEAKS", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=INK, pad=10)
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
The boxplot shows the summary. The violin shows the **shape**. Bimodality is the
story the box can't tell. *(Wilke 2019, Ch. 7)*
:::

<!-- slide 79 -->
## Ridgeline · the data {.smaller}

[Distributions · ridgeline build]{.eyebrow}

### How does the −log10(p) distribution change as |log2FC| grows?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Load the DESeq2 results and bin genes by `|log2FoldChange|`. Each bin gets its
own −log10(p) distribution; we'll stack them as a ridgeline so you can watch
the distributions march to the right as the effect size grows.

```python {code-line-numbers="1-5"}
de = load_deseq2()
de.head(3)
# →            gene  baseMean  log2FoldChange   pvalue       padj
# 0  Gene_00000     12.4         -0.21          0.40        0.62
# 1  Gene_00001     85.1          0.07          0.71        0.84
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
de = load_deseq2()
de.head(3)
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 80 -->
## Ridgeline · Step 1: bins + KDEs {.smaller}

[Distributions · ridgeline build]{.eyebrow}

### Bin by |log2FC|, KDE the −log10(p) inside each bin

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Cut |log2FC| into 5 bins, KDE the −log10(p) distribution within each, normalise
each density so the **shape** is comparable across bins of different size.

```python {code-line-numbers="1-13"}
from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde
de = load_deseq2().dropna(subset=["padj"])
de["nlp"]    = -np.log10(de["pvalue"].clip(1e-50))
de["absfc"]  = de["log2FoldChange"].abs()

bins = [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 4.0]
labels = ["<0.5", "0.5–1", "1–1.5", "1.5–2", ">2"]
de["bin"] = pd.cut(de["absfc"], bins=bins, labels=labels)

xs = np.linspace(0, 12, 300)
kdes = {lab: gaussian_kde(g["nlp"])(xs)
        for lab, g in de.groupby("bin", observed=True)}
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 4.7
from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde
de = load_deseq2().dropna(subset=["padj"])
de["nlp"]   = -np.log10(de["pvalue"].clip(1e-50))
de["absfc"] = de["log2FoldChange"].abs()
bins = [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 4.0]
labels = ["<0.5", "0.5–1", "1–1.5", "1.5–2", ">2"]
de["bin"] = pd.cut(de["absfc"], bins=bins, labels=labels)
xs = np.linspace(0, 12, 300)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.7))
for lab, g in de.groupby("bin", observed=True):
    if len(g) > 5:
        k = gaussian_kde(g["nlp"])(xs); k = k / k.max()
        ax.plot(xs, k, color=GREEN, lw=1.2, alpha=0.6, label=lab)
ax.set_xlabel("−log₁₀(p)"); ax.set_ylabel("density (normalised)")
ax.legend(title="|log2FC|", frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="upper right")
ax.set_title("STEP 1: BINS + NORMALISED KDEs", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=INK, pad=10)
plt.show()
```

<!-- slide 81 -->
## Ridgeline · Step 2: stack with the spectrum ramp {.smaller}

[Distributions · ridgeline build]{.eyebrow}

### One ridge per bin, coloured along the blue→teal→green→amber→red ramp

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Each ridge sits a little above the previous one; they overlap slightly so the
panel is compact. Bin colour comes from `econ_spectrum` so as the effect size
grows the band shifts cleanly along the ramp.

```python {code-line-numbers="1-11"}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5))
overlap = 1.6
n = len(labels)
for i, lab in enumerate(labels):
    k = kdes[lab]; k = k / k.max() * overlap
    col = econ_spectrum(i / (n - 1))
    ax.fill_between(xs, i + k, i, color=col,
                    alpha=0.75, lw=1, edgecolor=CREAM, zorder=i)
ax.set_yticks(range(n))
ax.set_yticklabels(labels)
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 5
from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde
de = load_deseq2().dropna(subset=["padj"])
de["nlp"]   = -np.log10(de["pvalue"].clip(1e-50))
de["absfc"] = de["log2FoldChange"].abs()
bins = [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 4.0]
labels = ["<0.5", "0.5–1", "1–1.5", "1.5–2", ">2"]
de["bin"] = pd.cut(de["absfc"], bins=bins, labels=labels)
xs = np.linspace(0, 12, 300)

    col = econ_spectrum(i / (n - 1))
    ax.fill_between(xs, i + k, i, color=col, alpha=0.75, lw=1, edgecolor=CREAM, zorder=i)
```

<!-- slide 82 -->
## Ridgeline · Step 3: the message {.smaller}

[Distributions · ridgeline build]{.eyebrow}

### Distributions march rightward as effect size grows

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
The story is in the shift: low-effect bins sit pressed against zero, then each
successive |log2FC| bin slides further right. The shape is the story; the
ridgeline lets the audience see it at a glance.

Many distributions in one compact panel, one continuous ramp keyed to bin order
so the eye can follow a single bin without a rainbow of unrelated hues.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 5
from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde
de = load_deseq2().dropna(subset=["padj"])
de["nlp"]   = -np.log10(de["pvalue"].clip(1e-50))
de["absfc"] = de["log2FoldChange"].abs()
bins = [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 4.0]
labels = ["<0.5", "0.5–1", "1–1.5", "1.5–2", ">2"]
de["bin"] = pd.cut(de["absfc"], bins=bins, labels=labels)
xs = np.linspace(0, 12, 300)
kdes = {lab: gaussian_kde(g["nlp"])(xs) for lab, g in de.groupby("bin", observed=True) if len(g) > 5}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5))
overlap = 1.6
n = len(labels)
for i, lab in enumerate(labels):
    if lab not in kdes: continue
    k = kdes[lab]; k = k / k.max() * overlap
    col = econ_spectrum(i / (n - 1))
    ax.fill_between(xs, i + k, i, color=col, alpha=0.75, lw=1, edgecolor=CREAM, zorder=i)
    # annotate where each ridge peaks
    ax.text(xs[np.argmax(k)] + 0.2, i + 0.4, lab, fontsize=8,
            color=INK, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_yticks(range(n)); ax.set_yticklabels(labels, fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("−log₁₀(p)"); ax.set_ylabel("|log2FC| bin")
ax.set_xlim(0, 12)
ax.set_title("STRONGER EFFECTS HAVE LOWER p — DISTRIBUTIONS MARCH RIGHT",
             fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=GREEN, pad=10)
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
Ridgeline = many distributions, one continuous ramp ordered by bin, so every
band is its own colour and the eye can still track the shift over time / effect.
:::
